section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
text: Organic additives play an important role in regulating fi lm growth and properties in Cu electrodeposition. 3‑Mercapto‑1‑propane sulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are representative accelerators that promote Cu electrodeposition rate. In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul fi de pairs by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy.

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
text: In this study, the formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS wa determined by measuring the equilibrium constants of thiol–disulfide interchange reactions with the reference thiol/disul fi de pairs by 1 H nuclear magnetic resonance (1H NMR) spectroscopy. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode).

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > ABSTRACT
text: The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS to MPS was 0.153 V (vs. standard hydrogen electrode). Based on this calculation, the cell potentials of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation reaction with either SPS or MPS, which is a key reaction in accelerating mechanism, were also estimated by ultraviolet–visible absorption and 1 H NMR spectroscopies: they were found to be 0.202 V and 0.214 V for SPS and MPS, respectively. The positive cell potential indicates that the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes is thermodynamically favorable in the presence of additives.

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
text: Cu has been widely used as metallization material in the semi conductor industry owing to its low electrical resistivity and high electromigration resistance. Cu metallization is usually performed by electrodeposition, which e fi ciently yields high quality fi lms by a relatively simple and inexpensive process. Electrolyte for Cu electrodeposition typically contains small quantities of organic additives, which are essential to regulate fi lm growth and properties. Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate.

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
text: Additives are grouped into accelerators, suppressors, and levelers according to their roles in controlling the deposition rate. Among them, 3‑mercap to‑1‑propanesulfonate (MPS) and its dimer bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) are the most representative accelerators in Cu electrodeposition [1]. The accelerating e f ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2].

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
text: The accelerating e f ect of SPS or MPS has been explained by two mechanisms [2]. One describes competitive adsorption between accel erator and suppressor; the displacement of suppressor inhibition layer by SPS or MPS facilitates the approach of Cu ions to electrode surface, enhancing the deposition rate [ 3 - 7 ]. The other mechanism focuses on direct catalytic reduction of Cu ^2 + ion to C u ^+ ion by forming Cu(I) (thiolate) complex [8–11]. The reduction of Cu ^2 + to Cu ^+ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12].

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 1. Introduction
text: The reduction of Cu ^2 + to Cu ^+ is known as the rate-determining step of Cu electrodeposition [12]. Vereecken et al. reported that the amount of C u ^+ near electrode surface is a key factor determining the deposition rate in Cu electrodeposition [13,14]. Nevertheless, only trace amounts of C u ^+ can exist in the electrolyte, as C u ^+ is easily oxidized to Cu ^2 + by dissolved oxygen. MPS or SPS in electrolyte can form stable Cu(I)(thiolate) complex, increasing the amount of C u ^+ species near the electrode surface [14]. The corresponding reactions are described as follows.

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 3.2. Formal reduction potential of SPS
text: As a pair of thiol/disul fi de, SPS and MPS can react with another thiol/disulfide pair via substitution, which is called thiol–disulfide interchange reaction [19–22]. The reduction potential of disulfide compound in thiol–disulfide interchange is usually obtained by establishing the equilibrium between the target material and a reference thiol/disul fi de pair of known redox potential, rather than electroanalytical measurements because many redox systems of sulfur are electrochemically irreversible [ 1 5, 1 7, 2 3, 2 4 ].

section: Thermodynamic aspects of bis(3‑sulfopropyl) disulfide and 3‑mercapto‑1‑propanesulfonic acid in Cu electrodeposition > 4. Conclusions
text: The formal reduction potential of SPS was fi rst determined by using thiol–disulfide interchange reaction with ME and Lip. The calculated formal reduction potential of SPS under the standard condition was 0.153 V (vs. SHE) in aqueous solution. The cell potential of the formation of Cu(I)(thiolate) complexes, which is the key reaction to explain the accelerating mechanism, was also estimated based on the formal reduction potential of SPS. The cell potential of Cu(I)(thiolate) formation between C u ^+ and SPS was 0.202 V, and the reaction between Cu ^2 + and MPS was 0.214 V.
